paragraphs.text: [Anxi](anxi:where-it-is) is a county in southern Fujian, inland from the coast and north of Xiamen, on the southern side of the Daiyun mountains. On this tea the name says [where the leaf grew](anxi:on-a-label), not its style or grade. The tea dates from 1988. Anxi was then still one of the poorer counties in Fujian, and the [Tieguanyin boom](anxi:history) that changed that had not yet come.

It was also made before the [light green style](tieguanyin:styles) took over in Anxi in the 1990s, at a time when the roasted style, the older of the two, still held. The trade has a name for Tieguanyin kept for years: chenxiang, or old Tie. This one is thirty-eight years old. The light kind goes stale quickly, and the heavier, charcoal roasted kind is the one [kept for years](tieguanyin:ageing), sealed, dry and dark, until the fire of the roast settles.

[Tieguanyin](tieguanyin:definition) is both a cultivar and the partly oxidised [oolong](oolong:definition) made from it. The leaf is rolled into tight balls by [wrapping it in cloth](tieguanyin:making), pressing it and drying it a little, again and again, with each round making it tighter.

brewing.text: Tieguanyin is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C; the light green style is often taken a little cooler, about 85 to 95°C. Use about 4 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 150 ml gaiwan or pot, about a third full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 10 to 30 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and a good Tieguanyin gives about six to eight. In a larger pot, use about 2.5 to 5 grams for 240 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: A smoother, rounder, softer cup with the fire gone, a liquor turned orange-red or reddish-brown, and often a soft fruity sourness.
